woman-as-other: In The Second Sex, Simone de Beauvoir argues that man has historically been treated as the default, the essential subject, while woman is defined only in relation to him as the "Other"—the inessential, the object against which he measures himself. This asymmetry, she contends, is not rooted in nature but produced and sustained by culture, myth, and social arrangement, so that femininity becomes a situation imposed rather than a destiny given. Understanding womanhood as Otherness exposes the mechanisms by which one group is cast as secondary and denied full standing as a free subject.
ethics-of-ambiguity: The Ethics of Ambiguity is Simone de Beauvoir's attempt to build a moral philosophy on existentialist foundations, taking seriously the claim that human beings have no fixed essence and must create meaning through their choices. She argues that freedom is the source of all value, but because we are always situated among others whose freedom matters as much as our own, genuine freedom requires willing the liberation of others rather than treating them as means. The ambiguity of the title names the human condition itself—we are at once free consciousness and bound flesh, subject and object—and ethics consists in embracing that tension rather than fleeing it into bad faith.
becoming-woman: "One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman" is Simone de Beauvoir's most famous line, marking her insistence that gender is not a biological given but a social and historical construction. On this view the traits taken to define femininity are instilled through upbringing, expectation, and constraint rather than dictated by anatomy, so that being a woman is a role one is shaped into rather than an essence one possesses. The claim helped separate sex from gender and became a foundational move for later feminist thought.
the-absurd: For Albert Camus, the absurd names the collision between the human craving for meaning, order, and clarity and a universe that offers no such answers in return. It is not a property of the world alone or of the mind alone but the confrontation between them, arising when a person who demands significance meets a silent, indifferent cosmos. Camus treats this recognition as the honest starting point for thought, and his central question becomes how to live fully once one no longer expects the world to justify existence.
sisyphus: In The Myth of Sisyphus, Camus takes the figure condemned by the gods to roll a boulder eternally uphill only to watch it fall as the emblem of the absurd human condition. Rather than despair, he argues that Sisyphus can be imagined happy: by consciously embracing his fate without illusion or hope of reward, he wrests a kind of freedom and dignity from a meaningless task. The essay is Camus's answer to what he calls the only serious philosophical problem, whether life is worth living, and it concludes that one can affirm life precisely in the face of its lack of ultimate meaning.
camus-revolt: Rebellion, for Camus, is the constructive response to the absurd: rather than surrendering to nihilism or false hope, the rebel says no to injustice and suffering while affirming a value shared with others. In The Rebel he distinguishes this metaphysical and moral revolt—which asserts human solidarity and sets limits—from revolution that sacrifices present lives to an abstract future and thereby betrays its own origin. Revolt thus becomes a way of creating meaning and holding to human dignity without appealing to any transcendent guarantee.
embodiment: Maurice Merleau-Ponty made the lived body central to phenomenology, arguing against views that treat the body as a mere object or the mind as a detached spectator. On his account we do not merely have bodies but are our bodies, and perception, movement, and understanding all flow from a bodily engagement with the world that precedes reflective thought. This notion of embodiment recasts consciousness as situated and incarnate, so that our grasp of space, other people, and meaning itself is grounded in the way our bodies are already at home in a perceived environment.
frankl-meaning: Drawing on his survival of the Nazi concentration camps, Viktor Frankl argued that the deepest human drive is not pleasure or power but the search for meaning, and that a person can endure almost any suffering if they can find significance in it. Logotherapy, the psychotherapeutic approach he founded, holds that meaning can be discovered through work and creation, through love and encounter with others, and through the attitude one takes toward unavoidable suffering. Even in conditions where everything else is stripped away, Frankl insists, the freedom to choose one's stance toward one's circumstances remains.
levinas-face: Emmanuel Levinas placed ethics before metaphysics, arguing that our most fundamental relation is not knowledge of the world but the encounter with another person. In this encounter the "face" of the Other confronts me with an infinite claim that I cannot reduce to my own categories or possess; it commands me and calls me to responsibility before I have chosen it. For Levinas this face-to-face relation is the origin of moral obligation, making responsibility for the Other the first fact of human existence rather than a consequence of contract or calculation.
turing-test: Proposed by Alan Turing in 1950, the Turing Test replaces the vague question "can machines think?" with a concrete behavioral test: if a human judge, communicating only through text, cannot reliably tell a machine's responses from a person's, the machine should count as intelligent. The proposal sidesteps disputes about inner experience by treating conversational indistinguishability as the criterion for thought. It has framed decades of debate in artificial intelligence and the philosophy of mind about whether behavior alone can settle questions of genuine intelligence.
chinese-room: John Searle's Chinese Room is a thought experiment designed to show that running a program is not sufficient for genuine understanding. He imagines himself locked in a room, following a rulebook to manipulate Chinese symbols and produce fluent replies without understanding a word of Chinese; the room as a whole passes for a Chinese speaker, yet no one and nothing inside grasps meaning. Searle uses the case to argue against "strong AI," contending that syntax—the formal manipulation of symbols—can never by itself yield semantics, the actual understanding of what symbols mean.
searle-intentionality: Biological naturalism is John Searle's account of how mind fits into the physical world: consciousness and intentionality are real, higher-level features of the brain, caused by neurobiological processes much as digestion is caused by the stomach. Intentionality is the mind's capacity to be about or directed at things—beliefs are about states of affairs, desires about outcomes—and Searle holds this aboutness to be an intrinsic, biologically grounded feature that cannot be reduced to mere symbol processing. The position aims to take consciousness seriously as a genuine phenomenon while denying both dualism and the claim that computation alone produces a mind.
brain-in-a-vat: The brain-in-a-vat scenario imagines that your brain has been removed and kept alive in a vat, fed electrical signals by a computer so that your entire experience of an external world is an elaborate illusion. It is a modern version of Descartes's skeptical doubt, raising the worry that you could never rule out such a predicament from the inside and so cannot be certain anything you perceive is real. Hilary Putnam gave the puzzle a notable twist, arguing on grounds of the theory of reference that the sentence "I am a brain in a vat" is self-refuting and cannot be true if uttered by an envatted brain.
twin-earth: In his Twin Earth thought experiment, Hilary Putnam asks us to picture a planet exactly like ours except that the substance there called "water" is not H2O but a different compound, XYZ, indistinguishable in everyday experience. Since a speaker on Earth and an identical counterpart on Twin Earth are in the same internal mental state yet their word "water" refers to different substances, Putnam concludes that meaning is not fixed by what is in the head. This argument for semantic externalism—captured in the slogan "meanings just ain't in the head"—holds that the reference of many terms depends on the actual environment and community, not on inner mental content alone.
hard-problem: David Chalmers coined the "hard problem of consciousness" to distinguish it from the comparatively easy problems of explaining cognitive functions such as perception, memory, and behavioral control. The easy problems concern how the brain performs tasks and can in principle be answered by ordinary science; the hard problem asks why there is subjective experience at all—why any physical process should be accompanied by an inner, felt quality rather than proceeding in the dark. Chalmers argues that even a complete functional account would leave this question of why experience exists unanswered, posing a deep challenge to purely physicalist theories of mind.
